essays.title: Making Startups Powerful
essays.thesis: A useful question to ask any startup is how it could become more powerful, which tends to unlock far bigger gains than asking how it could earn more.
essays.summary: Graham lists ways a startup gains power: owning the customer relationship, getting money to flow through it, network effects, going full stack, and spotting side features that could become the real product. He adds playing the long game, being generous, being extensible, and selling to young, fast-deciding customers. Startups are weakest where mafia-like incumbents control the market. Every route to power must also make things better for the customer, which is why new startups are good for the world.
key_ideas: Ask how a company could become more powerful, not just richer.
Network effects can often be added to products that seem not to have them.
Selling to early-stage companies gives startup-speed revenue growth and fast decisions.
Creating more value than you capture is the route to being very rich.
Tails that wag the dog: peripheral features can turn out to be the real product.
Power strategies only work if the customer ends up better off.

essays.title: How Universities Should Prepare Founders
essays.thesis: Universities prepare founders best by teaching real building skills, making startups feel possible, and leaving students free time for their own projects, not by teaching entrepreneurship.
essays.summary: Graham argues, drawing on what YC partners look for, that founders need to be good at building things and in the habit of doing so. Universities need only change two things: convince students that starting a startup is feasible, and give them room for self-directed projects, which supply knowledge, cofounders, and ideas. He says starting a startup cannot be taught in a classroom, and business plan competitions mislead students into thinking investors rather than users are the audience. The best approach looks too quiet and costs nothing.
key_ideas: Founders need building ability and a habit of building, not management training.
Seeing real founders makes startups feel both desirable and attainable.
Spare time, like Harvard's reading period, produces ambitious projects.
Business plan competitions train students to chase investors instead of users.
Giving students time lets energetic ones do far better while lazy ones do slightly worse.

essays.title: How to Earn a Billion Dollars
essays.thesis: Becoming a billionaire does not require cheating; it follows from exponential growth in a big market, which comes from making something users love.
essays.summary: Addressing future politicians at Oxford, Graham answers a claim that earning a billion is impossible by having the audience compute how few months of rapid growth turn millions into billions. Only two numbers matter, growth rate and how long it lasts, and neither depends on exploiting anyone. High growth comes from deeply understanding users, and young founders should build what they and their friends want. The best ideas come from side projects, not from hunting for startup ideas.
key_ideas: Wealth growing at a high monthly rate reaches a billion within months, not decades.
Growth rate and market size are the only two numbers that determine startup outcomes.
Word-of-mouth growth requires making something people truly love.
Young founders predict future demand through their own needs.
Best startup ideas sound lame at first and come from unplanned projects.

essays.title: How to Convert Between Wealth and Income Tax
essays.thesis: A wealth tax rate converts to an income tax rate by dividing by the return on capital, so a 1% wealth tax is roughly a 20% income tax.
essays.summary: Graham works through a short example with a 5% return to show that a 1% annual wealth tax takes the same amount as a 20% income tax. He notes politicians speak of a 'mere 1%' wealth tax yet would never call a 20% income tax hike mere. Adding that to typical US marginal rates would give the highest taxes in the world. He hopes politicians can be taught the conversion.
key_ideas: A wealth tax is an income tax divided by the rate of return.
At a 5% return, each 1% of wealth tax equals 20% of income tax.
The same conversion applies to capital gains versus annual taxation.
Few politicians appear to understand the scale of what they propose.

essays.title: The Brand Age
essays.thesis: When technology erases real differences between products, brand takes over, as the Swiss watch industry shows, and brand is opposed to good design and tends to produce a strange world.
essays.summary: Graham traces how the quartz crisis pushed Swiss watchmakers from engineering toward luxury branding, producing huge distinctive watches, artificial scarcity, and managed asset bubbles. Branding is centrifugal and design is centripetal, so distinctiveness costs quality. He names the present era the brand age and says quality becomes a threshold rather than a selling point. The lessons: avoid working on brand, and follow interesting problems, which leads you to golden ages.
key_ideas: Brand is what remains once substantive product differences vanish.
Branding seeks distinctiveness while good design seeks the single right answer.
Expensive watches grew bigger as they switched from telling time to telling brand.
Artificial scarcity only works when buyers want a brand over performance.
Fields have golden ages; follow problems rather than chasing prestige.

essays.title: The Shape of the Essay Field
essays.thesis: Writing for smart readers about important topics means writing for the young, because they are the ones who don't yet know what you have to tell them.
essays.summary: Graham divides reasons readers don't know something into unimportance, obtuseness, or inexperience. Essays about important topics therefore reach the inexperienced most. He frames essay impact as how much you change readers' minds times the importance of the topic, with a tradeoff between them that favours important topics for younger audiences. He doesn't plan to change his method of following curiosity, but wonders what important things people learn late.
key_ideas: Readers lack knowledge because it's unimportant, they're obtuse, or inexperienced.
Targeting smart people and important topics yields a young audience automatically.
Essay impact is change in thinking multiplied by topic importance.
Young readers allow bigger payoffs from important topics.

essays.title: Good Writing
essays.thesis: Writing that sounds good is more likely to be right, because fixing the sound improves the ideas and makes errors easier to spot.
essays.summary: Graham says sound and sense are linked, like shaking a bin so objects pack tighter: revising awkward passages never makes ideas worse. Because the writer is the first reader, smoother prose makes flaws noticeable. Good rhythm reflects the natural shape of a train of thought. A liar can write beautifully only by half believing a false premise, so beauty signals internal consistency rather than truth, though clumsy writing usually signals wrong ideas.
key_ideas: Sounding good and being right are connected, like a plane's shape and its flight.
Arbitrary constraints on wording tend to improve ideas.
The writer is the first reader and benefits from easy-to-read text.
Natural rhythm matches the shape of the underlying thought.
Beautiful prose proves consistency, not necessarily truth.

essays.title: What to Do
essays.thesis: One should help people, take care of the world, and make good new things, the last being the way to live to one's full potential.
essays.summary: Graham asks what one should do and proposes three principles, with making good new things as his addition. He defends it as the best proof of good thinking and says it biases toward creation over criticism. Traditional answers addressed how to be, not what to do, because few had choices. Now that many can pursue Archimedes-like work, making new things deserves a place in how to live, and amazing work often helps people anyway.
key_ideas: Making good new things is the best evidence of having thought well.
Newness matters; copying yourself repeatedly isn't impressive.
Older moral codes described how to be because audiences couldn't choose their work.
Unprestigious new kinds of work are often worth seeking out.
Amazing work often benefits the world unintentionally.

essays.title: The Origins of Wokeness
essays.thesis: Wokeness is an aggressively performative focus on social justice, a modern outbreak of the perennial priggishness that grew from academia and was amplified by social media; the remedy is treating it like a religion and resisting new heresies.
essays.summary: Graham dates political correctness to the late 1980s when 1960s radicals gained tenure, saw it fade, and revive in the 2010s through social media, polarised press, and a new class of administrators. He explains its virality via fear of impropriety and organisational capture. He says it is in retreat since 2020. Defence: apply the customs used for religion, and keep a standing bias against defining new heresies.
key_ideas: Every society has prigs; only their chosen rules change.
Orthodoxy that is shallow and complicated substitutes for real virtue.
Social media rewards outrage, which fuelled the second wave.
New bureaucrats whose jobs require finding problems keep it alive.
Treat wokeness like any religion within institutions.
The number of true things we cannot say should not increase.

essays.title: Writes and Write-Nots
essays.thesis: AI will leave a world of people who can write well and people who cannot, with the middle disappearing, which is dangerous because writing is thinking.
essays.summary: Graham predicts that since AI removes the pressure to write, most people will stop learning, much like manual strength faded after industrialisation. Writing is hard because it requires clear thinking, so it has been a forced skill. Skills disappearing is not always harmful, but here it costs a form of thinking. The result could be a split between those who think and those who don't, with strong thinkers being those who choose it.
key_ideas: Writing is hard because clear thinking is hard.
AI relieves the pressure that forced most people to learn writing.
The middle ground between good and non-writers will vanish.
Some thinking can only be done by writing.
Like physical fitness, thinking may become optional.

essays.title: When To Do What You Love
essays.thesis: Following your passion is wise in some situations and not in others, but if you want to do great work or build a huge startup, working on what interests you most is right.
essays.summary: Graham traces when interest and money align: strange tastes, intellectual interest in money, and startups where fun projects become big ideas. He describes a midwit peak for making money. When torn, you're usually ignorant of yourself, the work, and your ability, so try things early and choose options that keep future choices open. For great work, following interest is necessary.
key_ideas: Passion pays when few others share your lucrative tastes.
Making huge money favours working on what interests you.
Indecision usually reflects ignorance that experimentation can reduce.
Judge work by the colleagues you'd become.
Stay upwind: prefer options that keep more options open.

essays.title: Founder Mode
essays.thesis: Growing companies need a founder mode in which the CEO engages deeply beyond direct reports; standard manager-mode advice damages founder-led companies.
essays.summary: After Brian Chesky's talk, Graham explains why founders were told to hire good people and give them room, advice that nearly destroyed Airbnb. This describes managing a company you didn't found. Founders felt gaslit by advisors and by executives skilled at managing up. Founder mode will involve skip-level meetings and practices like Steve Jobs's retreats, though it remains poorly understood. He warns it will be misused.
key_ideas: Hire good people and give them room is manager advice that failed founders.
Founder mode breaks the rule that CEOs only talk to direct reports.
Business schools and books have not described founder mode.
Founders felt gaslit by VCs and senior executives.
Founder mode will likely be misused as an excuse for not delegating.

essays.title: The Right Kind of Stubborn
essays.thesis: The persistent differ from the obstinate: they are attached to the goal and flexible about methods, with energy, imagination, resilience, judgement, and focus.
essays.summary: Graham asks whether persistence and obstinacy are truly different and concludes they are. The obstinate resist changing ideas reflexively and cling to first ideas, whereas the persistent listen and revise low-level plans while staying committed to a high-level aim. He breaks persistence into five qualities and says obstinacy is simple and common while persistence is complex and rare.
key_ideas: Persistent people crave criticism; obstinate people glaze over.
Persistence attaches to goals high in the decision tree, not to details.
The persistent are boats with unthrottleable engines; the obstinate, boats with stuck rudders.
Five ingredients: energy, imagination, resilience, judgement, and goal focus.
Some obstinacy helps against panic but hurts on hard problems.

essays.title: The Reddits
essays.thesis: Y Combinator was partly founded to fund the Reddit founders, who were pushed from a bad idea to build Reddit, a site matching their curious, anti-authority personality.
essays.summary: Graham recalls meeting Steve Huffman and Alexis Ohanian before YC existed, rejecting their phone-ordering idea, and then proposing a link-sharing site. They launched quickly, grew slowly, and attracted Chris Slowe and Aaron Swartz. Reddit's personality is Steve's, and the site grew despite management neglect, and when Steve returned in 2015 it accelerated.
key_ideas: YC grew partly from wanting to fund these founders.
Their original idea was infeasible, so they pivoted to link sharing.
A launch version could be a couple of hundred lines of code.
Great startups closely match their founders' personalities.
Reddit was nearly unkillable thanks to a fundamentally useful product.

essays.title: How to Start Google
essays.thesis: Teenagers who might start a startup should build their own projects and do well in school, because projects supply technical skill, ideas, and cofounders.
essays.summary: In a talk to 14 and 15 year olds, Graham says you need technology skill, an idea, and cofounders. Projects deliver all three: they teach real skill, ideas appear when you see what's broken, and cofounders come from collaborating. Doing well in school matters because selective universities are where cofounders cluster. The best startup ideas begin as projects, like Facebook, Apple, and Google.
key_ideas: Build things yourself rather than consuming them.
Technical skill makes missing things visible as sticking doors.
Great startups began as projects not meant to be companies.
Make something you and friends want.
Selective universities concentrate cofounders and talent.

essays.title: The Best Essay
essays.thesis: The best essay would discover important surprising truths, and in practice good essays come from starting with a good question and rewriting strictly.
essays.summary: Graham starts by asking what the best essay would be and concludes it would describe a major discovery. He then asks how to write essays well. Start with a question and an edge, write a flawed first response, reread strictly, and follow branches with generality and novelty. Timeless essays require ideas that don't stick, so cover things people never learn. Writing many essays helps and more questions are the hardest thing to get.
key_ideas: The best essay concerns the most important topic you can surprise people on.
Writing turns vague ideas into bad ones, which can then be fixed.
Follow branches with the greatest generality and novelty.
Be quick to cut passages that cost effort but don't fit.
Evergreen essays cover things people never learn from culture.

essays.title: Superlinear Returns
essays.thesis: Returns for performance are superlinear because of exponential growth and thresholds, so ambitious people should seek compounding work and exceptional output.
essays.summary: Graham explains returns to performance, such as businesses, fame, and science, rise faster than effort through exponential growth and thresholds. He says to seek work that compounds, especially learning, and fields where a few outperform. Technology has reduced organisations' damping, widening this territory and variance. Curiosity is the best guide, and the most extreme returns come from expanding the territory.
key_ideas: Product half as good gets no customers, not half.
Two causes: exponential growth and winner-take-all thresholds.
Seek work that compounds and keep learning.
Declining institutions increase variation in outcomes.
Fields with big winners are those requiring independent ideas.

essays.title: How to Do Great Work
essays.thesis: Doing great work means choosing work with aptitude and deep interest, reaching a frontier, noticing gaps, and exploring them, sustained by curiosity, honesty, and morale.
essays.summary: A long recipe: pick a field by following excited curiosity, learn to the edge of knowledge, notice gaps, and explore them. He covers working technique, avoiding affectation, originality, choosing unfashionable problems, successive versions, risk, youth versus age, colleagues, morale, and copying. He concludes that curiosity is the guiding force and urges the reader to decide to try.
key_ideas: Choose work by aptitude, interest, and room for greatness.
Curiosity drives each step from field choice to exploration.
Originality starts with strictness and willingness to break rules.
Make successive versions and start small.
Guard morale, pick colleagues well, and be earnest.

essays.title: How to Get New Ideas
essays.thesis: New ideas come from noticing anomalies, especially gaps at the frontiers of knowledge.
essays.summary: Graham answers a question from a GPT trained on his essays. He says anomalies in everyday life help but frontiers are best, because knowledge grows fractally and its edges are full of gaps that seem obvious. Exploring them can yield whole new fields.
key_ideas: Notice what seems strange, missing, or broken.
The frontier of knowledge is the best place to find anomalies.
Knowledge's edges look smooth from afar but have gaps up close.
Exploring gaps can produce new fields.

essays.title: The Need to Read
essays.thesis: Reading remains necessary because it teaches writing, and writing is a way to have ideas, not only to convey them.
essays.summary: Graham says even if reading were replaced, we would lose a way to learn writing. Writing is a form of discovery that talking cannot fully replace. Complicated, ill-defined problems benefit from writing, so you can't think well without writing well, nor write well without reading well.
key_ideas: Reading teaches how to write as well as the content.
Writing discovers new ideas beyond what you already thought.
Complicated vague problems benefit from writing.
Those who want ideas can't just collect information.

essays.title: What You (Want to)* Want
essays.thesis: You can do what you want but cannot want to want what you want, at some number of levels of desire.
essays.summary: Graham resolves the puzzle of free will by refining a wrong slogan. People sometimes change what they want, so add 'want to', but it becomes rarer with each added level. The correct statement uses a repeating pattern, so ultimately a basic want exists that you don't control.
key_ideas: People can sometimes change what they want.
Changing higher-order wants gets progressively rarer.
Some deepest desire is outside your control.
The truth can be approached with repeated 'want to's.

essays.title: Alien Truth
essays.thesis: Alien truth, truths that intelligent beings would share, is a useful target for philosophy beyond math and physics.
essays.summary: Graham suggests besides math and physics, aliens might share principles like experimental evidence and Occam's razor. These give a target for truth. He links it to Erdos's book of proofs and says searching for them could define philosophy. AIs may eventually clarify the threshold.
key_ideas: Some truths beyond math would be shared by any intelligence.
Practice improving skill and Occam's razor could be shared.
The idea gives a target for general truths.
Err on the side of generosity when guessing.

essays.title: What I've Learned from Users
essays.thesis: Founders have much to learn from users; for Graham the lessons of YC are that startups share problems, founders misjudge priorities and ignore advice, and YC works through focus and colleagues.
essays.summary: Graham reflects on what he learned from YC's startups. Problems repeat across companies, yet advice must be individualised, as the batch that broke YC showed. Founders misjudge which problems matter, don't believe counterintuitive advice, and need focus to move fast. YC retrains founders from hacking the test, and the community of colleagues is its other great gift.
key_ideas: Most startups have the same problems.
Founders often don't recognise their biggest problem.
Counterintuitive advice sounds wrong, so founders don't listen.
Speed defines startups, focus enables speed.
Colleagues are as valuable as advice.

essays.title: Heresy
essays.thesis: Heresy has returned as a secular concept, in which an opinion is punished regardless of truth and outweighs everything else, driven by aggressive conformists and new ideologies.
essays.summary: Graham says opinions people are fired for have the structure of heresy. Labels like x-ist end discussion and apply depending on who speaks. Intolerant people always exist; they wave when an ideology unites them, as in the Cultural Revolution and campus politics since the late 1980s. The problem is the derivative: free expression has contracted. He hopes to build antibodies against heresy itself.
key_ideas: Heresy outranks truth and a person's whole record.
Whether a statement is x-ist depends on its speaker.
Aggressive conventional-minded people align behind ideologies.
The trend, not the level, of free expression worries him.
Aim to disable the concept of heresy.

essays.title: Putting Ideas into Words
essays.thesis: Putting ideas into words reveals they were incomplete, so someone who never writes has no fully formed ideas on nontrivial matters.
essays.summary: Graham says writing exposes imprecision, and rereading as a stranger shows gaps. Ideas feel complete until tested. Formal domains allow some mental work, but even experts learn from writing. Writing is stricter than talking. So those who don't write lack fully formed ideas and don't know it.
key_ideas: First words are usually wrong.
Reread as a neutral stranger to find gaps.
Half the ideas in an essay arise while writing.
Writing is the steeper hill compared to talking.
Without writing you can't know you lack formed ideas.

essays.title: Is There Such a Thing as Good Taste?
essays.thesis: There is such a thing as good taste, because denying it would mean denying good art, and responses to art are shared enough to be partly objective.
essays.summary: Graham uses reductio: without good taste there is no good art, so no good artists, which is absurd. His painting experience showed him the gap between himself and Leonardo. People doubt because opinions vary and experts err. Art works on shared human responses, like vaccines, giving a partial order of works and judges.
key_ideas: No good taste would mean no good art or artists.
Painting oneself shows the gap between skill levels.
Disagreement stems from extraneous influences on response.
Objectivity is a matter of degree based on shared human responses.
Taste has a partial order, not a perfect one.

essays.title: Beyond Smart
essays.thesis: What matters is having new ideas, not being smart, and its other ingredients such as interest, independent-mindedness, projects, hard work, and writing can be cultivated.
essays.summary: Graham says Einstein's distinction was new ideas, not intelligence. School fosters the illusion that smartness is what matters because it's measurable. Many smart people achieve little, so other ingredients exist, many of which can be cultivated. He lists obsessive interest, independence, techniques, hard work, and writing ability. The gap between intelligence and new ideas is worth mining.
key_ideas: Intelligence is a precondition for new ideas, not the same thing.
Childhood overrates intelligence because it is measurable.
Other ingredients can be cultivated, unlike mostly inborn intelligence.
Writing ability helps discover some ideas.
The gap deserves study.
coined_terms: gap between intelligence and new ideas

essays.title: Weird Languages
essays.thesis: Weird programming languages reveal the interesting 0.5% of programming beyond gluing library calls, so learning them expands how you think.
essays.summary: Graham says claims that all languages are equivalent reflect the work done. Most programming is glue code that popular languages handle equally. Good weird languages indicate other programming. Lisp macros, which allow writing a language for the problem, are his example. Learn a weird language whose users are smart.
key_ideas: Most programming is glue that all popular languages do.
Weirdness in good languages signals something distinctive.
Lisp macros enable building a language for the problem.
Learning to say new things teaches thinking new things.

essays.title: How to Work Hard
essays.thesis: Doing great work requires working very hard, which means learning what real work is, finding your limits, aiming at the hard core, and staying honest with yourself.
essays.summary: Graham says great work needs ability, practice, and effort. Learning to work without external goals starts with feeling that idleness is wrong. You must discount fake work in school and bogus jobs, find the daily hour limit, and aim at the center of problems. Choosing what to work on is ongoing for some. Honesty ties it together.
key_ideas: Great work needs talent, practice, and effort together.
Real work has a solidity that school often lacks.
Each kind of work has a daily limit beyond which quality falls.
Aim toward the true core of a problem.
Honesty about effort and results tunes the system.

essays.title: A Project of One's Own
essays.thesis: Working on a project of your own, voluntarily and with autonomy, is far more productive and exciting than ordinary work, and schooling steers us away from it.
essays.summary: Graham describes his son's excitement to introduce projects of one's own, like skating versus walking. Schools make work dutiful and mask the link between childhood play and adult work. Ownership means voluntary and solo, with softer edge into collaboration, as at the original Macintosh team. Autonomy matters, and kids teach us to start without fear.
key_ideas: Own projects are as different from ordinary work as skating from walking.
School hides the path from treehouses to real work.
Ownership means voluntary and, softly, by oneself.
Work/life balance misleads for people who skate.
Starting is where high standards hurt most.

essays.title: Fierce Nerds
essays.thesis: The nerds who are fiercely competitive, overconfident, impatient and independent-minded are increasingly the ones who win big, but they must channel that fierceness into ambitious work or it curdles into bitterness.
essays.summary: Graham profiles the fierce nerd, using Crick and Watson as the model, and lists the traits: competitiveness, confidence, intelligence, independence and impatience. He tells young fierce nerds the good news that more of the world is now winnable by being right, especially business. The bad news is that unused fierceness turns into trolling and hating. His remedy is to work on hard, ambitious projects rather than blunt the fierceness.
key_ideas: Nerds look meek only in social settings where they are out of their element.
Overconfidence is a self-fulfilling advantage up to a point.
Power has been shifting from dealmakers to technicians.
Unexercised fierceness turns into bitterness and hating.
Ambitious projects are the antidote to bitterness.
essays.stance: encouraging character sketch with a warning

essays.title: Crazy New Ideas
essays.thesis: Never dismiss a preposterous-sounding idea from a reasonable domain expert; its implausibility is more likely a sign of interest than error, so ask questions instead.
essays.summary: Graham argues that when a competent expert proposes something that sounds crazy, they presumably know something you don't, so the idea is a good bet on average. He lists why people dismiss such ideas anyway: envy, wanting to seem sophisticated, vested interests, factionalism, and above all the grip of the current paradigm. New ideas always look feeble at birth, so he recommends studying how past ideas began. The kind response is to encourage the lonely people who have them.
key_ideas: Implausibility from a competent expert is evidence of excitement, not incompetence.
Everyone is too conservative, including the people who have the new ideas.
Attacking new ideas is cheap and always looks clever.
The current paradigm erases the history of how it was once doubted.
Respond with questions, not verdicts.

essays.title: An NFT That Saves Lives
essays.thesis: A nonprofit he supports is auctioning an NFT whose proceeds directly save lives, at a very low cost per life.
essays.summary: Graham announces Noora Health's NFT, explaining that Noora teaches new mothers in South Asian hospitals and measurably reduces infant deaths. He cites its cost of about $1,235 per life saved. The NFT's novelty is that it gets better as the price rises, since each increment funds more saved lives.
key_ideas: Noora Health saves about nine babies per thousand births in its hospitals.
Its cost per life saved is the lowest he has seen.
The NFT will come with a public report on how the money is spent.
Here a higher price means more lives saved.

essays.title: The Real Reason to End the Death Penalty
essays.thesis: The real argument against the death penalty is not abstract morality but that the system routinely convicts innocent people, so in practice it kills the innocent.
essays.summary: Graham says debates about capital punishment focus on theory, yet at least 4% of people on death row are innocent. He recounts a string of exonerations and one execution that was later discredited. He blames sloppy or crooked police and prosecutors, weak defence lawyers, bogus experts and jurors who want closure. His conclusion is that the system's incompetence and dishonesty is the real issue.
key_ideas: At least 4% of death row inmates are innocent.
Wrongful murder convictions are common, not rare.
Police and prosecutors are under pressure to close high-profile cases.
Theoretical debates are moot when the process convicts the innocent.

essays.title: How People Get Rich Now
essays.thesis: Today's richest Americans mostly got rich by founding tech companies, which is a return to the historical norm that was suppressed by mid-century oligopolies, and it explains rising inequality.
essays.summary: Comparing the Forbes 100 of 1982 and 2020, Graham shows heirs, oil and real estate giving way to founders of tech companies. He argues that 1892 looked more like 2020 than 1982 did, because consolidation and big corporations made founding a company unviable for most of the 20th century. As those oligopolies broke up, startups got cheaper to start, founders gained leverage over investors, and companies grew faster. So of course the Gini coefficient rose: more people are starting more valuable companies.
key_ideas: Founders' equity is now the main source of new fortunes.
The mid-20th century was the anomaly, not the 21st.
Technology lowered the cost of starting and growing companies.
Founders now have more bargaining power over investors.
Faster growth makes founders' stock worth far more far sooner.

essays.title: Write Simply
essays.thesis: Write with ordinary words and simple sentences, because it is easier on readers, more honest, longer-lasting and more considerate.
essays.summary: Graham lists the benefits of simple prose: readers keep more energy for ideas, read further, and non-native speakers can follow. Fancy writing can hide a lack of ideas, while simple writing exposes it, and plain prose ages better. His own reason is aesthetic, since complicated sentences strike him as clumsy, and his method of fast drafting and long cutting also yields simplicity.
key_ideas: Simple prose leaves readers more energy for your ideas.
Fancy language can disguise having nothing to say.
Many readers are non-native English speakers.
Plain writing lasts better over time.
Heavy editing mostly means cutting.

essays.title: Donate Unrestricted
essays.thesis: Donors should give to nonprofits unrestricted, because restricting a gift means either the nonprofit is bad or the donor is overriding better judgement.
essays.summary: Graham explains that restricted donations are the nonprofit world's secret curse. If a nonprofit understands where money is needed better than the donor, the donor's restriction makes the gift worse. Exceptions are umbrella organisations like universities and expert donors like the Gates Foundation. Donors restrict gifts for publicity and habit, and nonprofits cannot afford to say so, so he says it for them.
key_ideas: A restriction implies either a bad nonprofit or the wrong use of money.
Umbrella organisations and expert donors are fair exceptions.
Donors often want credit or publicity as well as impact.
Nonprofits cannot talk back to big donors.

essays.title: What I Worked On
essays.thesis: Graham's career has been a messy chain of following curiosity and opportunity, with little foresight, through programming, painting, Viaweb, Y Combinator, essays and Lisp.
essays.summary: This memoir walks from his school-age programming and a disillusioning brush with AI to Lisp, art school, and then Viaweb, where he learned about users, growth and the low end eating the high end. He describes how Y Combinator grew out of ignorance, angel-investing instincts and the batch model, how he handed it to Sam Altman, and how he then painted, wrote essays, and spent years on Bel. A recurring pattern is that he did best on unprestigious things he found interesting, and that he usually did not know what he was doing.
key_ideas: Many of his best choices were accidents born of ignorance.
Working on unprestigious things guards against impure motives.
The low end of a market eats the high end.
Growth rate matters more than absolute numbers early on.
YC's batch model came from wanting practice as investors.
coined_terms: the low end eats the high end

essays.title: Earnestness
essays.thesis: Earnestness, meaning real interest in a problem for its own sake and trying as hard as one can, is the highest compliment for a founder and a strong predictor of success.
essays.summary: Graham says he and Jessica Livingston prize earnest founders, whose motives and effort are both right. Earnestness is the root of nerdiness and often looks like naivety, which has become an advantage as problems get harder than the ones in school. It matters less in fields near crime or politics. He ends by observing that money and genuine intellectual interest have become more aligned in business, which may be startups' most important change.
key_ideas: Earnest founders pursue the problem for its own sake.
Caring is both a strength and a social vulnerability.
Naive optimism can offset the rot of rapid change.
Check how much earnestness matters in a field by who wins there.
It is now easier to get rich working on what interests you.

essays.title: Billionaires Build
essays.thesis: To get funded by YC, show you understand a group of users who want what you are making, and be candid; this is also why billionaires are made by serving users rather than exploiting people.
essays.summary: Graham explains how YC partners guess whether there is a path to a huge market and whether the founders can find it. They probe who your first users are and how you know they want it, so interviews are random-access questioning, not pitches. Candour beats bluffing, and genuine interest in the project matters most. He then argues the same qualities produce billionaires, so the political claim that billionaires got there by exploiting people is wrong and harmful to social mobility.
key_ideas: The key question is how you know people want this.
Interviews are for random-access questioning, so don't turn them into pitches.
Answer candidly; bluffing is easy to detect.
Billionaires keep working because the company is their project.
Exploitative founders fail even on a small scale.
essays.stance: practical how-to with a political rebuttal

essays.title: The Airbnbs
essays.thesis: What made Airbnb special was how earnest its founders were: they did nothing halfway and never gave up despite no growth.
essays.summary: Graham recalls the founders' interview, their energy, and how close they were to quitting, with maxed credit cards and no growth in a recession. They persisted because their experience as first hosts showed them the future. During YC they chased ramen profitability by going to New York, meeting hosts and photographing listings, and growth finally arrived weeks into the batch.
key_ideas: The Airbnb founders were unusually energetic and open to advice.
They kept going because they had glimpsed something real.
Focusing on the hottest part of the market started growth.
Visiting hosts in person taught them about their users.
Ramen profitability was their milestone.

essays.title: How to Think for Yourself
essays.thesis: Some work only pays off if you think differently from your peers, and independent-mindedness, which has three components, is largely innate but can be cultivated.
essays.summary: Graham distinguishes work where you must be right and others wrong (science, investing, startups) from work where being right is enough, and urges choosing work by temperament. He offers ways to boost independence: know fewer conventions, choose independent friends, read history and watch for intellectual fashions. He decomposes independent-mindedness into fastidiousness about truth, resistance to being told what to think, and curiosity, and says curiosity is the one to cultivate.
key_ideas: Choose work by whether it requires thinking differently.
People misjudge how conventional they are.
Surround yourself with a few independent-minded people.
Independence needs care about degrees of belief or it becomes conspiracy theory.
Follow what you are curious about.

essays.title: Early Work
essays.thesis: Fear of making something lame stops great work, because early versions of ambitious projects look feeble, so we must learn to judge them differently.
essays.summary: Graham says people are too harsh on early drafts of new ideas, both others' and their own, and that Silicon Valley has built customs that treat odd ideas as challenges. For your own work he suggests overestimating its importance, slight overconfidence, ignorance, supportive colleagues and teachers, focusing on rate of improvement, and calling it a sketch. The ultimate fix is to learn that early versions really are worth more than they seem.
key_ideas: Many great projects look unimpressive early on.
Silicon Valley has a custom of optimism toward strange ideas.
Slight overconfidence offsets harsh self-judgement.
Treat early work as a sketch or quick hack.
Study the feeble first steps behind great work.

essays.title: Modeling a Wealth Tax
essays.thesis: A wealth tax compounds on the same assets year after year, so even small rates take huge fractions of a founder's stock over a lifetime.
essays.summary: Graham models a wealth tax on a founder who lives sixty years after building a company. A 1% tax takes 45% of stock and a 2% tax takes 70%. Adding a $50 million threshold and growth assumptions barely helps, because the tax is applied repeatedly to the same asset.
key_ideas: A 1% annual wealth tax takes about 45% of stock over 60 years.
A 2% tax takes about 70%.
A high threshold only partly mitigates this.
Income tax hits each year's income once, but a wealth tax hits the same asset repeatedly.

essays.title: The Four Quadrants of Conformism
essays.thesis: People can be classified on two axes, conventional versus independent and passive versus aggressive, and societies prosper by protecting the independent-minded from the aggressively conventional.
essays.summary: Graham sketches four types seen even among schoolchildren: tattletales, sheep, dreamers and naughty kids. He argues one's quadrant comes from personality rather than era, so today's aggressively conventional would have defended slavery. Enlightenment customs retired heresy to guard against them, but those customs are now weakening, driven partly by social media and universities. The independent-minded, who produce new ideas, are the canaries, and will build new institutions.
key_ideas: Conformism varies along conventional-independent and passive-aggressive axes.
Personality decides your quadrant more than the society you live in.
Banning bad ideas also restricts closely related good ones.
Enforcers of orthodoxy compete to be stricter.
Independent thinkers will found new institutions if universities fail.

essays.title: Orthodox Privilege
essays.thesis: Conventional-minded people suffer from 'orthodox privilege', the blind belief that it is safe for everyone to say what they think because it is safe for them.
essays.summary: Graham coins the term and says it makes people unable to imagine true statements that get you in trouble. He reasons that in every past era there were such statements, so it would be a coincidence if ours had none. Unlike other privileges it cannot be fixed by learning more, so he suggests appealing to politeness: take people at their word, as you would about a sound you cannot hear.
key_ideas: The conventional-minded feel safe saying whatever they believe.
Every era has had unsayable truths.
Orthodox privilege resists correction by information.
Politeness suggests believing people who report unsayable truths.

essays.title: Coronavirus and Credibility
essays.thesis: A fast, unambiguous event like an epidemic exposes pundits who confidently predict things they do not understand, giving us a rare accurate test of credibility.
essays.summary: Graham watched commentators say the coronavirus would be no worse than flu and noticed they thought they could never be caught. Normally predictions are vague or distant enough to escape accountability, but an epidemic falsifies them quickly. He urges remembering who was wrong now.
key_ideas: Pundits usually get away with false predictions.
An epidemic checks predictions quickly and plainly.
This is a rare clean test of credibility.

essays.title: How to Write Usefully
essays.thesis: A good essay should be useful: correct, important, novel and strongly stated, and you get there by publishing only what you're sure of.
essays.summary: Graham defines usefulness as the product of four qualities and explains how to achieve each using yourself as a proxy for the reader. He describes his loose-then-tight drafting, deletion of weak sentences and attention to qualification. Novelty and strength make people angry and prone to misrepresent you. He recommends starting with narrow topics and notes that nearly all essays remain unwritten because the internet only recently opened the form.
key_ideas: Useful writing is true, important, novel and strongly stated.
Delete any sentence you don't believe rather than publishing it.
Qualification is a skill that expresses degrees of certainty.
Novelty provokes people because it contradicts cherished beliefs.
Most essays are still unwritten.

essays.title: Being a Noob
essays.thesis: Feeling like a noob is a sign you are doing something novel, so the more you feel it locally, the less ignorant you are globally.
essays.summary: Graham notes he constantly feels like a beginner in new fields and countries. He argues the feeling correlates inversely with true ignorance. Our dislike of it is an evolutionary relic from a stable world, like our taste for food in an age of abundance, and misleads us now.
key_ideas: Feeling like a noob signals exposure to something new.
Staying in familiar territory means less discomfort but less knowledge.
Our aversion evolved for an unchanging world.
The more a noob you feel, the better.

essays.title: Haters
essays.thesis: Haters are just fanboys with the sign flipped: obsessive, uncritical and best handled by not thinking about them.
essays.summary: Graham explains that fame produces fans who idolise you and haters who despise you in identical ways. Haters tend to see their target as a fraud, are often frustrated talents who have achieved little, and never do great work themselves. Because they are not people you have a dispute with, there is no use trying to understand or appease them.
key_ideas: Fame produces obsessive fans and obsessive haters in symmetrical ways.
Haters see the famous as frauds.
People who do great work don't become haters.
Don't treat a hater as an opponent in a dispute.

essays.title: The Two Kinds of Moderate
essays.thesis: Accidental moderates, who reach the middle by making up their own minds, differ from intentional moderates, who just pick the midpoint, and are the most impressive and courageous.
essays.summary: Graham distinguishes two types by the spread of their opinions. Intentional moderates acquire positions in bulk like ideologues and shift with the median. Accidental moderates choose their own questions and answers, and are attacked from both sides. People working with ideas who intersect with politics have to be accidental moderates or mediocre.
key_ideas: Intentional moderates choose the midpoint on every question.
Accidental moderates' opinions scatter but average to the middle.
Both extremes and intentional moderates take opinions in bulk.
Being openly an accidental moderate takes courage.

essays.title: Fashionable Problems
essays.thesis: Even smart people crowd into fashionable problems, so look for unexplored space in fields thought to be played out, and love what you do to resist fashion.
essays.summary: Graham observes that only a small fraction of possibilities get explored because everyone works on similar things. He suggests hunting in apparently exhausted fields like essays, Lisp and venture funding, where a new approach has huge surface area. Loving the work is the best protection against fashion.
key_ideas: Only a sliver of the possibility space gets explored.
Smart people still follow fashions in what to work on.
Fields thought fully explored may hold the most.
Genuine love of the work protects against fashion.

essays.title: Having Kids
essays.thesis: Having kids, which he dreaded, turned out to be wonderful, though it does cost productivity and perhaps ambition.
essays.summary: Graham says his pre-parent fears came from biased samples: noisy kids on airplanes and his own bad childhood. He describes the moments of peace, the friendship and the fun, and admits chemistry helped change his mind. He concedes kids shrink the time and attention left for work and may reduce ambition, but he found workarounds and still counts more happy moments than before.
key_ideas: Before kids he judged parenthood from selection-biased observations.
Kids give many moments when nowhere else feels better.
They become interesting friends.
Kids force you to work on a schedule.
They can make you less ambitious because attention is zero-sum.

essays.title: The Lesson to Unlearn
essays.thesis: The most damaging thing school teaches is to win by hacking bad tests, a habit that misleads founders and shapes our whole attitude to work.
essays.summary: Graham argues that grades have been conflated with learning and that tests imposed by authority are easily hackable, college admissions most of all. He noticed young YC founders always looked for tricks to raise money or get users instead of making a good product, and traced this to their schooling and his own. Tests not imposed by authorities are unhackable, and modern work increasingly rewards good work over test-hacking. He hopes people and schools will unlearn the habit.
key_ideas: Studying for tests diverges from learning.
Tests imposed by authorities are usually hackable.
College admissions is a very hackable test of taste.
Founders over-complicate because school trained them to look for tricks.
Startups are largely unhackable; you win by doing good work.

essays.title: Novelty and Heresy
essays.thesis: Discovering something new often draws accusations of heresy, and every cherished mistaken belief leaves a dead zone of unexplored ideas around it, which makes looking for heresies a way to find new ideas.
essays.summary: Graham reasons that new discoveries often hide behind mistaken assumptions people love. Suppressing heresy therefore also suppresses all nearby ideas. He ends by flipping the point: dead zones are mines for anyone seeking new ideas.
key_ideas: Non-obvious good ideas often sit behind a cherished mistake.
Heresy hunts suppress ideas that merely imply the mistake.
The more preposterous the belief, the larger the dead zone.
Looking for heresies is a way to find new ideas.

essays.title: The Bus Ticket Theory of Genius
essays.thesis: Great work comes from natural ability, determination and a third ingredient: a disinterested obsession with something that matters, which he calls the bus ticket theory.
essays.summary: Graham describes bus ticket collectors and argues that people like Darwin and Ramanujan began with obsessive, pointless-seeming interest. Such obsession is a proxy for ability, a substitute for determination, and leads to paths others overlook. Risk and reward interact, so some obsessions turn out useless, as with Newton's alchemy. He draws implications: interest explains uneven achievement, parenthood reduces it, and one should stay irresponsible and encourage kids to go deep.
key_ideas: Great work needs obsessive, disinterested interest in something that matters.
Obsession substitutes for determination and gives luck an edge.
You can't know in advance which obsessions matter.
Ambitious people may do better by working on what is just fun.
Interest is more unevenly distributed than ability.

essays.title: General and Surprising
essays.thesis: The most valuable insights are general and surprising, and with the most general ideas even a small novelty is worth pursuing, so don't be afraid of repeating yourself.
essays.summary: Graham says general and surprising together is rare, so most people get one without the other. A promising route is to add a small novelty to a very general idea. Because the generality multiplies value, it is not true that nothing is new under the sun, only that there is almost nothing.
key_ideas: The best insights are both general and surprising.
Gossip is surprising but not general; platitudes the reverse.
A small novelty on a general idea can be valuable.
Don't worry about repeating yourself on general topics.
Don't be discouraged by 'not much new'.

essays.title: Charisma / Power
essays.thesis: Powerful but uncharismatic people attract dislike, and being a target for criticism can mean someone is the right person, not the wrong one.
essays.summary: Graham says power draws criticism that low charisma cannot disarm, citing Hillary Clinton and builder-type CEOs. He sees no solution beyond recognising it.
key_ideas: Power draws criticism.
Without charisma it can't be deflected.
Builder CEOs face this.
Being criticised can signal the right person.

essays.title: The Risk of Discovery
essays.thesis: Newton's mistakes and risky bets in alchemy and theology are overlooked in biographies, but they were as promising to him as physics, which suggests great work involves real risk.
essays.summary: Graham argues biographies edit out scientists' mistakes, hiding their risk-taking. Newton's alchemy and theology looked as promising then as physics. He made three risky bets and one paid off.
key_ideas: Biographies trim mistakes and mask risk.
Newton's three obsessions looked equally promising at the time.
Smartness and craziness may not be separate.
One of Newton's three bets worked.

essays.title: How to Make Pittsburgh a Startup Hub
essays.thesis: Pittsburgh can become a startup hub by becoming more of what already makes it good: attracting young people with cheap, characterful housing, preserving its buildings, being walkable and tolerant, and having a great university.
essays.summary: In this talk Graham says he was won over by a report of a youth-driven food boom, since startups are made of people aged roughly 25 to 29. He advises encouraging independent restaurants, preserving old buildings, becoming bicycle and pedestrian friendly, making CMU great and otherwise staying out of the way, and tolerating strangeness. The missing piece is investors, which will come slowly, though cheaper startups, Kickstarter and YC reduce the need.
key_ideas: Startups need a magnet for people in their twenties.
Cities once rich and now poor offer palaces for cheap.
Universities help most by being great and getting out of the way.
A hub must tolerate all strangeness.
An investor community grows slowly and organically.

essays.title: Life is Short
essays.thesis: Life really is short, so you should prune bullshit, not delay things that matter, and savor the time you have.
essays.summary: Graham says having kids let him turn time into countable events, showing that life is short. He argues 'life is too short for x' deserves force. Bullshit enters either by force or by trickery, and he recommends avoiding it, asking what you will care about later, and being impatient about what matters. He ends by urging savoring, using his mother's death as an example.
key_ideas: Kids make the shortness of life concrete.
Bullshit is the junk food of experience.
Fake importance has a sharp peak but small area.
Don't wait on what matters; there's no need for morbid reminders.
Pay closer attention to time to savor it.

essays.title: Economic Inequality
essays.thesis: Economic inequality has many causes, some bad and some good, and treating it as one thing leads to wrong remedies, so we should aim at problems like poverty and theft rather than at inequality itself.
essays.summary: Graham says writers treat inequality as a single phenomenon, often with the pie fallacy. He argues you must study individual rich and poor people. Creating wealth is a source that grows with technology and cannot be removed without killing startups. He accepts a rising baseline of inequality and says we should address its symptoms, like poverty and low mobility, and stop the crooked ways to get rich.
key_ideas: The pie fallacy assumes the rich take from the poor.
Wealth creation differs from taking in kind and practice.
Variation in productivity is the irreducible core of inequality.
You can't remove great wealth variation without eliminating startups.
Aim at poverty and mobility, not inequality.

essays.title: The Refragmentation
essays.thesis: Rising fragmentation in politics, culture, cities and income is the unwinding of mid-century cohesion that came from war and big corporations, an anomaly that cannot and should not be repeated.
essays.summary: Graham says World War II and the big national oligopolies compressed American society economically and culturally. He describes the uniformity of mid-century TV, work and prestige, and how big companies underpaid executives and overpaid unions. As deregulation, global markets and computers broke the oligopolies, employees moved towards market pay, creating yuppies and wider inequality. The fragmentation is a reversion to the mean and should be mitigated, not reversed.
key_ideas: War and corporate oligopolies compressed society in the 20th century.
Mid-century conformity was no utopia.
Computers lowered coordination costs and loosened big firms.
Pay moved toward market price, increasing variation.
Technology's lever means variation in productivity keeps rising.

essays.title: Jessica Livingston
essays.thesis: Jessica Livingston is central to YC's success because she defined its culture, judged character with her Social Radar, and made its alumni network, but her dislike of attention has written her out of the story.
essays.summary: Graham counters the 'one-man show' description of YC. He describes it as a family with Jessica as its mom, whose culture was the product. Her gift for spotting fakers selected founders who were good people, which built the alumni network. She avoids attention and fighting, so the press ignores her, though she knows more about founders than anyone.
key_ideas: YC's culture was Jessica's innovation.
Her Social Radar sees through fakers.
Rejecting dubious characters cost little because good founders do better.
Her aversion to attention hides her role.
Founder quality predicts how startups do.

essays.title: A Way to Detect Bias
essays.thesis: You can detect bias in a selection process by checking whether the selected group in question outperforms the others, without knowing the applicant pool.
essays.summary: Graham explains that if applicants of type x face bias, those who get through must be better. So measure performance among those selected. As an example, First Round's finding that female-founder companies outperformed implies bias against them. He predicts more such analyses.
key_ideas: Biased selection makes the disfavoured group's survivors outperform.
The test needs measurable performance and similar ability distributions.
This is essentially what bias means.
Third parties can run the test using selected data alone.

essays.title: Write Like You Talk
essays.thesis: Writing in spoken language makes it easier to read, so don't let a sentence through unless you'd say it to a friend.
essays.summary: Graham says people switch into stilted written dialect. Spoken language is simpler and more direct, and fancy phrasing lets you think you are saying more. His fixes are checking each sentence, reading aloud, and explaining the draft to a friend.
key_ideas: Written English is often a different dialect from spoken English.
Complex ideas don't need complex sentences.
Experts speak more informally on harder topics.
Read drafts aloud and fix what doesn't sound like talking.

essays.title: Default Alive or Default Dead?
essays.thesis: Founders should know whether their startup is default alive or default dead, and should not hire too fast.
essays.summary: Graham says half the founders he meets can't say whether current growth and spending get them to profitability. Not asking leads to the fatal pinch. Investors are fickle, so fundraising is only plan A. The easiest way to avoid default death is not to hire too fast, since overhiring is the biggest killer of funded startups.
key_ideas: Default alive means reaching profitability on current trends.
Start asking too early rather than too late.
Always have a written plan B for funding.
Spending and growth are only weakly related.
Overhiring is the biggest killer of funded startups.

essays.title: Why It's Safe for Founders to Be Nice
essays.thesis: Founders can safely be nice because great products compound while rapaciousness only scales revenue by a constant, so growth rate is the number to optimise.
essays.summary: Graham explains using numbers that if you charge users half as much but keep your growth rate, you are only a few months behind. A slightly better growth rate overtakes the rapacious founder. Since startups win by making things people recommend, rapacity doesn't help and may hurt.
key_ideas: Extracting less money only scales a growth curve down by a constant.
Optimise the growth rate rather than extraction.
Startups win by word-of-mouth quality.
Niceness is a safe trade for working hard on growth.

essays.title: Change Your Name
essays.thesis: A US startup without the .com of its name should probably change it, because a marginal domain signals a marginal company.
essays.summary: Graham says founders resist renaming through identity and lack of imagination. Neutralise the first by imagining you had a different name, and the second by admitting you are bad at naming. Almost any decent word or word pair is good enough, so buy domains and choose.
key_ideas: A missing .com signals weakness.
Attachment to a name comes from it being yours.
Naming is a separate skill from being a good founder.
Most decent words work as names.
Nearly all top YC companies own their .com.

essays.title: What Microsoft Is this the Altair Basic of?
essays.thesis: Nearly every great company looked silly at launch, so when an idea seems lame, ask which giant company it could be the humble first step of.
essays.summary: Successful startups such as Microsoft, Airbnb and Facebook all began with ideas that looked not just small but wrong. Founders were often drawn to them by instinct without being able to explain why. Rather than mocking a lame-sounding idea, PG treats it as a puzzle: what Microsoft is this the Altair Basic of? There is often an answer the founders have not yet seen, sometimes several, and he advises following whichever is most exciting.
key_ideas: Almost all huge startups seemed lame or ridiculous when they launched
Founders often follow instinct without being able to articulate why the idea will grow
Mocking odd-sounding startup ideas is the default reaction, even among experts
Asking what bigger company a small idea could grow into turns doubt into a puzzle
A single startup can contain several possible giant companies of very different sizes
coined_terms: What Microsoft is this the Altair Basic of?

essays.title: The Ronco Principle
essays.thesis: Ron Conway shows that in a transparent, unpredictable world the most successful investors are the genuinely good ones, because goodness can no longer be faked cheaply.
essays.summary: PG describes Ron Conway as the most connected angel in the Valley and as unfailingly decent, and notes that his power came from his goodness because deals reach him by referral. He argues that investors used to be able to seem good without being good, but that transparency and unpredictability now make inconsistency costly. Mistreating a founder gets around, and you cannot tell which random kid will be the next star, so you must be nice to everyone. The trend, he suggests, extends well beyond startups.
key_ideas: The most successful startup investors tend also to be the most upstanding
Referrals bring Conway deals, and his reputation for goodness earns the referrals
Transparency makes bad investor behavior get out quickly among founders
Unpredictability means you cannot know whom it is safe to treat badly
Seeming good is increasingly impossible without actually being good

essays.title: What Doesn't Seem Like Work?
essays.thesis: If something that feels like work to other people does not feel like work to you, that is a strong sign of what you are suited to do.
essays.summary: PG uses his mathematician father, who treated textbook exercises as the reward rather than the chore, as an example of someone who knew early what he loved. Most people have to work out their calling from subtle clues, like a detective. A useful heuristic is to notice what seems like work to others but not to you, such as his own liking for debugging. The stranger your tastes look to others, the stronger the evidence they point to your path.
key_ideas: Tasks that others find painful but you find pleasant reveal your aptitude
Working out what to work on often takes detective-like inference
The stranger your tastes seem to others, the better evidence they are
Enjoying something tedious like debugging may be necessary to be good at programming
Ask yourself explicitly what seems like work to others but not to you

essays.title: Don't Talk to Corp Dev
essays.thesis: Young startups should not take meetings with corporate development people unless they truly want to sell right now, because the process is distracting and manipulative.
essays.summary: Corp dev is the part of a big company that buys other companies, so any meeting with them is about selling. PG says talking is only sensible when you are doing very badly or very well; for companies in the middle, it is a distraction that saps morale and tempts founders with imagined prices. Corp dev staff are measured on how cheaply they buy, so lowball offers and last-minute retrades are common. The simplest defense is the Rockefeller trick of never taking the first drink: decline the first meeting.
key_ideas: Corp dev exists to buy companies, so every meeting is about selling
Only talk to them if you want to sell right now and expect an acceptable price
Wishful thinking and flattery lure founders into taking pointless meetings
Acquirers use lowball offers and late retrades to wear founders down
Declining the first meeting is the safest protection and causes no offense

essays.title: Let the Other 95% of Great Programmers In
essays.thesis: Because over 95 percent of potential great programmers are born outside the US, restricting immigration of exceptional programmers harms the country and costs nothing to fix.
essays.summary: PG rebuts the claim that Americans can simply be trained to fill programming jobs: competent programmers can be trained, exceptional ones cannot, and the gap between them is enormous. Tech firms bother with visa contortions and pay immigrants normal salaries, which shows genuine scarcity. Exceptional performance in any field implies immigration for a country with a tiny share of world population. With talent increasingly mobile and clustering in hubs, the US risks losing its lead unless it keeps letting in a few thousand great programmers a year.
key_ideas: Great programmers differ from competent ones in kind, not just speed, and cannot be trained
Firms pay immigrants the same as Americans, so the shortage claim is credible
With under 5 percent of world population, most great people are born abroad
Talent could cluster in one foreign hub if the US turns people away
Letting in a few thousand great programmers yearly costs almost nothing

essays.title: How to Be an Expert in a Changing World
essays.thesis: Expertise goes stale as the world changes, so protect yourself by assuming change, staying open-minded, and betting on people who generate new ideas.
essays.summary: Experts are often wrong because they know an earlier version of the world, and confidence that rises with experience only makes sense for things that do not change. PG says startup investing taught him to guard against obsolete beliefs: believe explicitly in change, avoid hardening hypotheses, take your odd hunches seriously if you are expert, and turn comments into public bets. He also advises focusing on earnest, energetic, independent-minded people rather than ideas, which is how YC funded Airbnb. Change is accelerating, so the problem will only get harder.
key_ideas: Experts are often experts on an earlier version of the world
Explicitly assume the world is changing rather than static
Do not try to predict the future; stay sensitive to signs of change
Weird hunches from domain experts are worth exploring
Betting on earnest, independent-minded people beat judging ideas at first sight

essays.title: How You Know
essays.thesis: Reading and experience change your mental model of the world even when you forget the details, so forgetting what you read is not wasted effort.
essays.summary: PG worried that reading hundreds of books left him remembering almost nothing, then realised that what matters is how the reading altered his model of the world. Like a compiled program whose source is lost, the mind works without remembering why. This implies rereading important books is valuable because each reading is compiled by a different brain. He speculates that future technology may let us replay, index and even edit our experiences.
key_ideas: The harvest of reading is your changed mental models, not retained facts
The mind is like compiled code whose source has been lost
Rereading is worthwhile because the same book is processed differently at different times
Replaying recorded experience could become a way to learn from it again
Not knowing how you know things may not be permanent

essays.title: The Fatal Pinch
essays.thesis: A startup with a few months of money left, high spending and mediocre growth is in a fatal pinch because it will almost certainly not be able to raise more, and must fix its own finances.
essays.summary: PG names the situation where a startup with some cash but weak growth expects to raise again and is deluded about it: spending is higher, investor standards are higher and the company now reads as a failure. Prevention is to treat any raise as the last. Once in the pinch, assume the chance of raising is zero and choose among shutting down, cutting costs (usually people) or earning more. He recommends switching to making money differently, such as consultingish work for customers who will pay a lot, while avoiding the slippery slope into pure consulting.
key_ideas: Founders overestimate how easily they can raise a second round
Each additional round faces higher spending, higher standards and a failure default
Act as if the last money raised is the last you will ever get
In the pinch, assume zero chance of funding and fix cost or revenue
Consultingish work can rescue revenue if done mercenarily and without hourly billing

essays.title: Mean People Fail
essays.thesis: Successful people in startups and similar fields are rarely mean, because the games that matter are shifting from zero-sum fights over scarce resources to creating new things.
essays.summary: PG notes how few of the most successful people he knows are mean, and offers reasons: meanness makes you stupid, mean founders cannot recruit the best people, and benevolence helps fuel the drive to build great things. Historically success meant controlling scarce resources through fighting, so meanness paid. Now, with civil order and protection of what people create, more games are about new ideas, as they long were for thinkers. He concludes that being mean now makes you fail, and teaches his kids accordingly.
key_ideas: Few of the most successful people PG knows are mean
Fighting makes you stupid because it rewards case-specific tricks, not big ideas
Mean founders cannot attract the best people who have other options
Benevolent motives help founders keep going past tempting acquisition offers
Games are becoming non-zero-sum, reversing the old link between meanness and success

essays.title: Before the Startup
essays.thesis: Because startups are counterintuitive, would-be founders in college should not start one but instead learn deeply, indulge curiosity and live at the leading edge so good ideas and cofounders arise naturally.
essays.summary: Adapted from a Stanford lecture, the essay lists six counterintuitive points: trust instincts about people but not about startups; domain and user expertise matter more than startup expertise; gaming the system stops working; startups are all-consuming; you cannot tell in advance whether you can do it; and the way to get ideas is not to think of ideas. Young founders often play house by imitating the form of a startup. PG advises against starting one in college and instead recommends learning powerful things, working with people you respect on interesting problems, and getting to the leading edge of some technology. His boiled-down advice is: just learn.
key_ideas: Startup instincts mislead, but instincts about people are worth trusting
Know your users and problem, not startup mechanics
Playing house means copying startup rituals instead of making something people want
Startups consume your life, so starting at 20 forecloses valuable exploration
You cannot predict who will be tough enough; the only test is trying
The best preparation for a startup is curiosity-driven learning

essays.title: How to Raise Money
essays.thesis: Fundraising is best handled as a simple disciplined process: avoid investors until you decide to raise, then talk to them in parallel, treat non-commitments as noes, accept good offers quickly and get back to work.
essays.summary: This long guide explains the fears that drive investors, then gives rules for raising a seed round: stay out of fundraising mode until ready, get introductions, hear no until a definite yes, and run a breadth-first search weighted by expected value. It covers getting the first commitment, closing the money, avoiding investors who do not lead, having multiple plans, underestimating the raise, preferring profitability, not over-weighting valuation, and accepting offers greedily. Further rules include limiting dilution, letting one founder handle fundraising, not getting addicted, being nice and remembering that the bar is higher next time. The overall message is not to complicate it.
key_ideas: Investors are pinched between fear of flops and fear of missing hits
Be either fully in fundraising mode or not at all, since it consumes attention
Treat investors as saying no until they give an unequivocal commitment
Talk to investors in parallel, prioritised by likelihood times size of yes
Needing money makes it harder to raise; profitability gives leverage
Valuation matters far less than getting the money and good investors
coined_terms: breadth-first search weighted by expected value

essays.title: Investor Herd Dynamics
essays.thesis: Investors' opinions of you depend mostly on other investors' opinions, so fundraising has self-reinforcing momentum, though that momentum does not signal startup quality.
essays.summary: PG explains the forces behind stampedes of investor interest, not how to create one. Having raised money genuinely makes a company a better bet and justifies a higher price, success builds founder confidence that investors sense, mediocre investors follow the crowd because they are poor at judging startups, and good investors respond to deadlines created by competing interest. He warns against bluffing or revealing which VCs you are talking to. Most startups face the reverse: the herd stays distant, so the first commitment is hardest and the second easier.
key_ideas: Investor interest compounds as one investor's offer attracts others
Raised money truly makes a company more valuable and lowers its risk
Mediocre investors treat other investors' interest as the signal
Do not tell a VC which other VCs you are talking to
The first commitment is hardest; do not be demoralised by the initial hole

essays.title: How to Convince Investors
essays.thesis: The way to convince investors is not a polished pitch but to make a startup genuinely worth investing in, understand why, and explain it truthfully.
essays.summary: PG compares pitching to lifting with your legs rather than your back: let the startup do the work. Investors seek the rare big winner, judging whether founders seem formidable, the market is big and capturable, and there is some evidence of progress. Inexperienced founders should not imitate swagger but convince themselves first by honestly evaluating whether the startup is worth investing in, which requires domain expertise. When rejected, explain candidly why investors were mistaken. The recipe: make something worth investing in, understand why, then explain it clearly.
key_ideas: Investors treat outcomes as a power law and look for a chance at being a big winner
Formidable means justifiably confident, and investors decide quickly
Truth is the safest source of confidence for inexperienced founders
Founders need domain expertise to judge whether their startup is worth backing
Investors view startups as markets, so identify a plausible path to a big one
Be candid about rejections rather than evasive

essays.title: Do Things that Don't Scale
essays.thesis: Startups usually take off because founders do laborious things that don't scale, especially recruiting users by hand and delighting them.
essays.summary: PG says founders must start their startups like cranking an engine, since growth rarely happens on its own. He gives examples: Stripe's Collison installations, Airbnb's door-to-door work, Wufoo's handwritten notes. Further techniques include launching to a deliberately narrow market, building hardware yourself, acting like a consultant for one user, and doing manually what software will later do. Big launches and partnerships usually do not work. He proposes thinking of ideas as a vector: what you'll build plus the unscalable things you will do to get going.
key_ideas: Founders must make startups take off, usually by recruiting users manually
Small absolute numbers hide the power of compound weekly growth
Early startups are fragile and should not be judged by established standards
Aim for an insanely great experience of being your user, even with a buggy product
Contain the fire: start with a narrow market where you can win completely
Big launches and partnerships rarely produce growth

essays.title: Startup Investing Trends
essays.thesis: Cheaper startups and the normalisation of founding will give founders the upper hand, grow the number of big hits and reward investors who adapt, especially at the earliest stage and the series A.
essays.summary: Written for investors, the talk argues that startups are becoming cheaper and more normal, a third career path alongside jobs and grad school. Founders will keep more equity and control, but the number of really good startups will grow faster than the share sold, so top investors may earn more. The business shifts from an obelisk to a pyramid, with more early-stage opportunity. PG sees angel-sized investments made quickly, and series A rounds that start from what the company needs rather than the share VCs want, as the big unexploited openings.
key_ideas: Startups are becoming both cheaper and a normal career option
The famed 15 big hits a year is limited by the number of good founders, not ideas
Founders keep more control, and investors make more as founders' supporters
Early failures will widen the base so the startup business becomes a pyramid
Fast-deciding angel investors could win access to the best deals
Series A rounds sized by VC ownership targets are at odds with founders
Look for what founders complain about to find investing opportunities

essays.title: How to Get Startup Ideas
essays.thesis: The best startup ideas come from noticing problems you yourself have while living at the leading edge of something, not from trying to think up startup ideas.
essays.summary: PG says good ideas are something founders want, can build and few others see as worthwhile, and that made-up sitcom ideas sound plausible but have no urgent users. He describes demand shaped like a deep well for a small group with a path out. The route is to become the sort of person who has such ideas: live in the future, build what's missing, and turn off the filters of schleps, unsexiness and fear of competition. He then gives recipes for when you need an idea now, but says the organic approach is far better.
key_ideas: Solve problems you have yourself, so you know they exist
Made-up startup ideas sound plausible but yield zero real users
Narrow, deep demand beats broad shallow demand at the start
The verb is notice, not think up
Schleps and unsexy fields hide good ideas, and competition is rarely fatal
Live in the future and build what seems interesting

essays.title: The Hardware Renaissance
